prompt.context: Our client, Dr. Rossman, has invented an amazing product. He has discovered the chemical formula for Magic Eye Drops. One drop in each eye will cure short- or long-sightedness in any patient. Dr. Rossman is a scientist, not a businessman, and he has come to our firm because he wants to sell the rights to his Magic Eye Drops to a business that will commercialize the invention. Dr. Rossman has secured an exclusive, worldwide patent for the next 20 years. After the patent expires, generic versions will quickly be developed. Obstacles to regulatory approval are not foreseen. The Magic Eye Drops have no known side effects or risks.
prompt.question: What should Dr. Rossman's asking price be for the rights to his Magic Eye Drops?

clarifying_info.a: Focus only on corrective lenses (glasses and contacts) as competitors for the purposes of this case. Laser surgery is the closest competitor but can be set aside.
Focus only on the US market.

clarifying_info.q: What is the discount rate to use for NPV?
clarifying_info.a: Disregard discount rates for the purposes of this case — assume a discount rate of 0%.

clarifying_info.q: What is the annual growth rate of the market?
clarifying_info.a: Assume a projected annual growth rate of 3.5%, which by the rule of 70 means the market doubles before the patent expires.

exhibits.title: Costs
exhibits.shows: A table listing cost drivers and their associated costs for commercializing Magic Eye Drops over the patent life

data.Marketing: $150M per year for first 10 years; $50M per year for last 10 years

framework: Frame as a valuation / NPV problem: asking price = NPV of future revenues minus NPV of future costs
Estimate market size: size the US population with correctable vision problems by age cohort, apply adoption rates
Determine pricing strategy: competitive pricing vs. cost-based vs. value-based; anchor to annual cost of corrective lenses (~$200/year)
Project total revenues over 20-year patent life: market size × annual price × patent years
Estimate total costs over 20-year patent life from Exhibit 1
Calculate asking price: total revenues minus total costs (at 0% discount rate)

questions.prompt: Estimate the US market size (number of customers who would adopt Magic Eye Drops)
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the US population (~300M total, ~50M per age cohort of roughly 6 cohorts) by rate of sight problems and rate of adoption. Strong answers explain why adoption is lower among young children (eyes still changing, parental caution) and the elderly (fewer years of savings). Bonus for noting market growth: at 3.5% annual growth the market doubles over 20 years, so effective market size is ~100M customers.

math.setup: Divide US population into 6 age cohorts of ~50M each; apply rate of sight problems then rate of adoption.
steps: With 3.5% annual growth (rule of 70: doubles in 20 years), effective market ≈ 100M customers

questions.prompt: What price should be charged per treatment, and what is total revenue over the patent life?
questions.guidance: Candidate should consider competitive pricing (anchoring to ~$200/year cost of corrective lenses), value-based pricing (convenience factor pushes price up; newness/risk factor pushes it down), and cost-based pricing. Reasonable adjustments to the $200 anchor are acceptable. Revenue = market size × annual price × patent life. Candidate may note that not all customers buy immediately and adjust years downward.

math.setup: Market Size × Annual Value of Magic Eye Drops × Patent Life = Total Revenue

questions.prompt: What are the total costs over the patent life? Use Exhibit 1.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate each cost driver separately and sum them. Management/Overhead is 33% of other operating costs (Marketing + Production + Distribution), so those three must be calculated first.

math.setup: Calculate Marketing, Production, Distribution subtotals; then Management/Overhead = 1/3 × (Marketing + Production + Distribution); sum all four.
steps: Marketing: $150M × 10 yrs + $50M × 10 yrs = $1.5B + $0.5B = $2B (casebook simplifies as $100M avg × 20 yrs = $2B)

questions.prompt: What should Dr. Rossman's asking price be?
questions.guidance: Simple subtraction of total costs from total revenues (at 0% discount rate). Candidate should state the answer clearly and note the simplification.

math.setup: Asking Price = Total Revenue − Total Costs

recommendation: Dr. Rossman should list his invention at approximately $392B, representing the NPV of ~$400B in revenues less ~$8B in total costs over the 20-year patent life at a 0% discount rate

This assumes competitive pricing at $200/year (the annual cost of corrective lenses), a US addressable market of ~100M customers (accounting for 3.5% annual market growth), and a one-time treatment per customer
risks: Discount rate simplification understates true cost of capital — actual NPV would be lower
Not all customers will adopt immediately; spreading purchases over the 20 years reduces realized revenue
Riskiness of a new drug product may require a lower price point than the $200 competitive anchor
Post-patent generic competition may erode residual value
Actual production cost per drop could differ significantly at scale
next_steps: Solicit buyers, focusing on strategic acquirers (large pharma, medical device companies)
Attempt to start a bidding war among multiple potential buyers
Present at industry conferences and investor events to publicize the value of the invention
Refine NPV model with actual discount rate once a buyer's cost of capital is known
